A woman came to me once with a cracked wrist and a story about a fall that didn't match the shape of the break. I set the bone. I never once asked her to explain the story.

My aunt taught me my first real cure - a fever tonic, three ingredients, guarded like a family jewel - and made me swear never to write it down. I wrote it down that same night, in a letter, to a stranger three towns over whose daughter was burning up. I never told my aunt. I'm telling you instead.
I sang in a square in a town whose name I've let go of, for a crowd of exactly four people and a dog that howled along on the high notes. It remains one of my favorite performances.

A boy broke his leg falling out of the tallest tree at Velmora, the same week I arrived. I mended it, then sat with him three more evenings after, for no reason the bone required. He didn't understand why I kept coming back. Neither did I, entirely, at the time.

I taught a healing charm to a farmer's wife who had never held a wand in her life and had no business, by any account I was raised on, learning it at all. She used it on half the village before the season was out. My family would have been horrified. I have never been prouder of anything.

Mordy asked me once, very late, why I bothered with an old man who couldn't pay me in anything but company. I told him company was the payment. He didn't believe me for months. He believed me by the end.

There is a particular kind of quiet that settles over a room right before someone finally says the thing they've been carrying alone. I have learned, over a very long life and a longer death, simply to wait it out.

I once treated a burn with nothing but steady hands and an old song, because the herbs I needed were a day's walk away and the pain wasn't going to wait that long. I don't know which one did more good. I've never been sure it matters.
My mother kept a locked cabinet of remedies and a look on her face whenever I asked what was in it. I built my whole life as the opposite of that cabinet. I regret exactly none of it.

A girl at Velmora once asked me why I never sing anymore, in the sense she meant it - out loud, on a stage, for a room. I told her some things you don't stop doing, you just start doing them differently. I'm not certain that was entirely honest. I let her believe it anyway.

I sat with a dying woman once who spent her last clear hour worrying about who would feed her cat. I promised her I would. I have kept stranger promises than that one, and none that mattered more to keep.

Somebody asked me, long ago, what the trick was to healing so many people without ever once being paid for it. There isn't a trick. There's only the noticing, and then the going to them. Everything after that takes care of itself.

I remember a night early on at Velmora when I couldn't sleep either, and I sang half a verse to an empty hallway just to hear it exist somewhere besides inside my own head. I never finished the verse. I still haven't.
The best remedy I ever gave anyone had nothing in it at all - just a chair pulled close, and enough time that they stopped waiting for me to leave.
